item.title: Keyamo Flags Off Kogi International Airport Construction
item.description: The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo (SAN), on Tuesday joined the Governor of Kogi State, Ahmed Ododo, to officially flag off the construction of the Kogi International Airport at Zariagi, declaring that the landmark project will place the state on the global aviation map and open up new frontiers of economic opportunities. A statement by Tunde Moshood, Special Adviser on Media and Communications to the Minister, noted that Keyamo, who was accompanied by the NCAA’s Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection, Michael Achimugu, and other top aides, participated in the historic ceremony alongside the Governor, members of the State Executive Council, traditional rulers, other dignitaries and the immediate past Deputy Governor of Kogi State, Edward David Onoja. Keyamo Flags Off Kogi International Airport Construction on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. Speaking at the event, Governor Ododo described the airport project as a strategic investment in the economic future of Kogi State, emphasising its potential to unlock the state’s enormous agricultural and solid mineral resources for local and international markets. The Governor noted that Kogi State possesses immense economic potential which, if properly harnessed, could position it as a major contributor to Nigeria’s export economy. He explained that the airport would provide a significant boost to the transportation of agricultural produce and mineral resources, attract investors, stimulate commercial activities and create employment opportunities for the people of the state. He further highlighted the airport’s capacity to facilitate the movement of people and goods, strengthen connectivity, attract new businesses and accelerate the development of supporting infrastructure across the state. In his remarks, Keyamo described the flag-off as a historic milestone whose significance would endure for generations. “What is happening here today, what the Governor has done today, will resonate many, many years, centuries after today, 500 years from today. Do you understand the significance of what is happening here today? Let me tell you the significance. Today, as from today, this village called Zariagi will be on the Global Aviation Map,” the Minister declared. He explained that every recognised airport around the world is identified through a global aviation coding system, noting that the establishment of the airport would give Zariagi international visibility within the aviation community through the relevant identification and coding processes of the International Air Transport Association (IATA). According to him, the project represents a significant step in putting Kogi State on the global aviation landscape and connecting it to the wider world. item.title: Big Names Missing As World Leaders Take Stage At COP31
item.description: World leaders will take the stage at COP31 in Turkey on Wednesday, but some prominent names are missing from this year’s annual UN climate summit even as global warming intensifies. The two-week conference kicked off earlier this week in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with governments under pressure to tackle the climate crisis after a year of heatwaves in Europe, deadly floods in Nepal and major wildfires in Indonesia. Dozens of leaders will speak during the “high-level segment” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian. But observers have pointed to the absence of some big names, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit. While European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen is coming to Antalya, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping the event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the most recent list. “It is a shame that some of the bigger European leaders aren’t coming. We need Europe to be showing up strongly at this COP,” Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think-tank E3G, told AFP. Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s top climate official, said the absences were “not completely atypical” as leaders may have “practical” reasons for not being able to attend a summit. Climate activists sing during a demonstration organized by Climate Action Network (CAN) Europe at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on November 10, 2026. But he also told reporters in Brussels that “expectations are not necessarily high” for this climate conference. Iran’s Pezeshkian said he would use the event as an opportunity to express Tehran’s position on environmental destruction in war. “At this conference, we will speak about the actions of the United States and Israel in destroying the environment,” he said before departing for Turkey, according to Iranian state television. The French government said Macron would be absent because November 11 is World War I Armistice Day and the president will attend an EU summit in Ireland on Thursday. “If top leaders want influence over where the global (energy) transition is going, showing up is a pretty good place to start,” said Chiara Martinelli, director of Climate Action Network Europe. “I am afraid that Ursula von der Leyen will be lonely on the stage while the leaders of the biggest EU economies are a no-show,” Martinelli said. Swedish activist Greta Thunberg arrives at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on November 10, 2026. item.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, November 11, 2026
item.description: The US dollar is trading at approximately ₦1,350 per dollar at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM), while the naira exchanges at between ₦1,411 and ₦1,419 per dollar in the parallel market on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. Available exchange rate reports indicate that the official market rate was around ₦1,350.36 per dollar on Tuesday, November 10, while parallel-market dealers quoted buying and selling rates of approximately ₦1,411 and ₦1,419, respectively. At the parallel market, also known as the black market, the exchange rate varies depending on the location and the Bureau De Change (BDC) operator. The latest reported parallel-market figures indicate that Nigerians selling $1 to currency dealers could receive approximately ₦1,411, while those purchasing $1 may pay about ₦1,419. At the official market, the NFEM rate remains the benchmark for foreign exchange transactions in Nigeria. The difference between the reported official rate of ₦1,350.36 and the parallel market selling rate of ₦1,419 is approximately ₦68.64 per dollar. The exchange rate may change during the day depending on dollar supply, demand and trading activities across the foreign exchange market. Nigerians are advised to confirm prevailing rates with their banks and licensed currency dealers before carrying out foreign exchange transactions. item.title: Market conditions: Dangote Cement rescinds plan to list shares on London Stock Exchange
item.description: By Peter Egwuatu Dangote Cement Plc, has rescinded plan to list its shares on the London Stock Exchange, LSE following market conditions. The company disclosed this after its Board Meeting held on Tuesday. In a statement sent to the Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX and signed by Edward Imoedemhe Company Secretary, stated: “ This is to inform the Exchange, investing public and all stakeholders that at the meeting of the Board of Directors of Dangote Cement PLC held today, 10 November 2026, the Board resolved that, in light of current market conditions and the company’s strategic priorities, the company announces that it and its selling shareholder, Dangote Industries Limited (DIL) will not proceed with the proposed secondary listing and offering on the London Stock Exchange at this time. “ The company’s ordinary shares remain listed on the NGX, and this decision does not in any way affect the company’s operations or business plans. “Dangote Cement PLC remains focused on delivering sustainable value to its shareholders and building on its strong market position.” It will be recalled that Dangote had disclosed plans to list the cement business on the London Stock Exchange in May, eight years after an earlier attempt in 2018 failed. He had told the Financial Times that the proposed dual listing would involve selling about 10 percent of Dangote Cement’s shares on the UK exchange. item.title: Duke seeks opposition’s unity
item.description: •Warns against repeating 2023 mistakes, 1966 crisis •PRP unveils manifesto, makes candidates sign accountability pact By Clifford Ndujihe & Luminous Jannamike PRESIDENTIAL candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party, PRP, Mr Donald Duke, has urged opposition parties to unite ahead of the 2027 general elections, warning that failure to learn from the mistakes of 2023 could have grave consequences for Nigeria’s democracy. Read Also: Donald Duke: From Cross River record to PRP’s 2027 presidential gamble Duke, who spoke on Tuesday in Abuja at the unveiling of the party’s manifesto, A Compact for Nigeria’s Renewal, cautioned that opposition parties must rise above personal ambitions and differences to defend the country’s democratic foundations. He expressed doubts about the possibility of free and fair elections under the prevailing political circumstances, alleging that the President Bola Tinubu-led administration was deploying state institutions and other mechanisms to weaken opposition parties. “What should be clear to us all, the players and the electorate, is that we would be foolish to expect a free and fair electoral process, what some may term a level playing field. This will not happen, was never planned nor intended to happen,” he said. Warning against repeating the political miscalculations of 2023, the former Cross River State governor said: “We erred in 2023 and we are repeating the same in 2027. It is said, fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me. The shame will certainly be on us.” He called for strategic thinking and unconventional approaches by opposition forces to confront what he described as an unguarded political establishment. “David did not defeat Goliath in a wrestling bout, but by strategy and unconventional means,” he said. Duke alleged that opposition parties were being frustrated through restrictions on access to public venues, advertising opportunities, political intimidation and the use of state institutions. He also questioned the credibility of the electoral process, alleging that more than 10 million artificially generated voters had entered the register of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). ‘Nigeria risks another 1966 crisis’ He warned that the political situation could degenerate into a crisis reminiscent of the events preceding the 1966 military intervention if opposition parties failed to collectively resist alleged abuses of power. The PRP candidate also criticised the administration’s economic policies, arguing that widespread hardship, insecurity, rising taxes, electricity and transportation costs, and declining purchasing power should not be passed off as reforms. “It is only in Nigeria that hardship is termed reform,” he declared. On the proposed opposition coalition, Duke said political alliance-building must begin with agreement on a common vision for the country rather than merely negotiating who should emerge as presidential candidate. item.title: 2027 countdown: Obi pledges to unite Nigeria, tackle insecurity, poverty
item.description: • No Nigerian should remain in IDP camp if I become President • We’ll hunt down kidnappers, ensure safe return of displaced persons — Obi • Every voter must protect, monitor and ensure transmission of votes •Don’t allow politics to worsen insecurity, Gbong Gwom Jos warns By Golok Nanmwa JOS — Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr Peter Obi, has pledged to unite Nigeria, tackle insecurity and lift millions of citizens out of poverty if elected President in 2027. Read Also: Obi, who spoke at a town hall meeting with supporters in Jos, Plateau State, on Tuesday, said national unity, security, economic recovery and accountable leadership would be the priorities of his administration. “Our number one commitment is to unite the Federal Republic of Nigeria because today we have no unity. We are divided along tribal and religious lines. That should not be. We are Nigerians,” he said. The former Anambra State governor identified security as another major priority, promising to end the killings, kidnappings and displacement of citizens across the country. “Number two is to secure Nigeria. It is our duty to ensure that Nigerians live in safety, in a country where people are no longer killed daily. “I assure you that no mother will continue to cry over the loss of her children. No woman should experience the pain of losing her husband, and no father should suffer the agony of losing his wife,” he said. On internally displaced persons, IDPs, Obi declared that his administration would prioritise their safe return to their ancestral communities. “If any Nigerian remains in an Internally Displaced Persons camp, we have failed. Once one Nigerian is in an IDP camp, the entire Nigeria is in an IDP camp. People must return to their homes,” he said. He vowed that kidnappers and other criminal elements would face decisive action. “Nobody will kidnap two children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you,” he warned. Obi, who recalled visiting troubled communities in Bokkos, Barkin Ladi and Mangu local government areas of Plateau State, said the plight of victims of violence informed his presidential ambition. “If I have one person in an IDP camp, it means we are all in an IDP camp. I am competing because I want to know how we talk to that mother whose child was killed, that husband who lost a wife and that woman who lost a husband. Who is going to listen to their cries?” he asked. He said the town hall engagements were designed to make leadership demand-driven by allowing citizens to articulate their needs rather than merely listening to campaign promises. “When you want to serve, you must listen to the people. When we come for campaigns, we only talk and we don’t listen to the people. We have decided that leadership must be demand-driven,” he said. item.title: Leave politics to politicians, northern minorities tell clerics
item.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 general elections, the Northern Nigeria Minorities Group, NNMG, has cautioned religious leaders, particularly imams and pastors, against partisan political involvement and the use of churches and mosques as platforms for political mobilisation. The group, which represents more than 200 minority communities across Northern Nigeria and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), urged religious leaders to distinguish their spiritual responsibilities from partisan political activities, warning that inflammatory political messages from religious platforms could heighten tensions and expose Nigerians to violence. Addressing journalists in Abuja yesterday, the Convener, Jacob Edi, also known as Kakaki Bassange, said religious leaders should focus on praying for the peace and unity of the country, while leaving partisan politics to politicians. He said: “Politics is for politicians, religion is for pastors and imams. They should pray for this nation. They should pray for the peace and unity of Nigeria. “When a pastor or an imam tells you about peace, he is not looking for your vote. He is not even looking for your money. This is his duty. This is his calling.” Edi said anyone interested in partisan politics should relinquish religious leadership and join a political party to pursue such ambitions. “If he wants to come into politics, he should remove the garment or remove the jalabia or whatever and go to any party,” he said. The group also cautioned opposition politicians against actions capable of destabilising the country, urging them to resolve political disagreements through constitutional and judicial processes. item.title: Where are the meters?
item.description: The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) has approved a N30 billion disbursement to electricity distribution companies (DisCos) for the procurement and installation of meters under the meter acquisition fund (MAF) tranche C scheme. According to Order No NERC/2026/121, issued on Monday, the fund targets the provision of free meters to all remaining unmetered Band A customers and accelerating installations for Band B consumers. The commission had approved N21 billion for the first tranche and N28 billion for the second tranche of the initiative. In the order, NERC said the funding would be shared among the 11 electricity distribution companies (DisCos) in proportion to their respective contributions to the fund. NDC alleges plot to disrupt Obi’s visit to Benue Nigeria’s states have more money. Are they spending it well? Daily Trust reports that since the introduction of reforms in the electricity sector under the President Bola Ahmed Tinubu administration, the federal government has granted approval for the procurement of N1.116trn worth of prepaid meters for distribution to consumers for free. The reform, which saw the removal of electricity subsidy for Band A electricity customers, was meant to provide free meters for customers under the band, with extension to others in Band B, C, D and E. But despite the approval and release of funds, the rollout of the meters has been slow. Though the government maintains that the country has 12,747,789 electricity customers with 8,045,565 customers metered and 4,704,224 unmetered, many Nigerians still pay for their meters to stop alleged extortion by electricity Distribution Companies (DisCos) through estimated billing. To reduce reliance on estimated billing and improve electricity-sector revenue collection, the government introduced new schemes worth N1.11trn from 2024 to date. The distribution has largely focused on Band A customers, whom the former Minister of Power, Adebayo Adelabu, said made up 15 percent of electricity consumers. Daily Trust reports that the schemes the government introduced include the Distribution Sector Recovery Program (DISREP), Meters Acquisition Fund (MAF) and Presidential Metering Initiative (PMI). A breakdown of the money allocated to each scheme showed that DISREP allocated $250m (N337bn at N1348.10/dollar) for 3.2m meters, MAF got N79bn and PMI was allocated N700bn. While the DISREP and MAF are ongoing, PMI will start next year, but the funds have been released to the agency spearheading it. What the metering schemes entail DISREP is a $500 million World Bank loan aimed at improving the financial and technical performance of DisCos. One of the major objectives of DISREP is to close the metering gap in the NESI by deploying 3.2 million smart meters. Installation of meters under the DISREP commenced in May 2025. item.title: Nigeria’s private sector foreign debt rise 179.6% to $54.5bn — World Bank
item.description: By Babajide Komolafe The World Bank said that the foreign debt of Nigerian companies rose by 179.6 per cent in seven years to $54.48 billion in 2025 from $19.49 billion in 2018. This implies that Nigerian businesses now owe foreign lenders almost three times what they owed in 2018. The World Bank disclosed this in its International Debt Report 2026 which stated that Nigeria’s private sector nonguaranteed external debt stood at $54.476 billion as of December 2025. The World Bank explained that the total external debt of a country is the sum of public and publicly guaranteed debt, private nonguaranteed debt, and short-term debt. According to the World Bank, private sector nonguaranteed external debt refers to money borrowed by private companies from foreign banks, investors and other lenders without the government or any public institution guaranteeing repayment. “Private nonguaranteed debt comprises long-term external obligations of private debtors that are not guaranteed by a public entity. “Public and publicly guaranteed external debt comprises long-term external obligations (maturities of over one year) of all public debtors, including debt held by the central government and by state-owned enterprises. Short-term debt is defined as debt with an original maturity of one year or less ,” the report said. The 179.6 per cent growth in Nigeria’s private sector in the seven years was faster than the increase in government-backed external debt, which rose by 155.5 per cent from $24.422 billion in 2018 to $62.4 billion in 2025. The World Bank report showed that private companies’ foreign debt is becoming an increasingly important part of Nigeria’s external debt burden. In 2018, private sector nonguaranteed debt was equivalent to about 79.8 per cent of public and publicly guaranteed external debt. By 2025, it had increased to 87.3 per cent. Meanwhile, Nigeria’s total external debt, covering government borrowing, private companies’ foreign loans and short-term obligations, increased from $46.238 billion in 2018 to $145.015 billion in 2025. The report also highlighted the high cost of borrowing from private foreign lenders. According to the World Bank, new loans obtained by Nigeria from private foreign creditors in 2025 attracted an average interest rate of 9.6 per cent, compared with 1.9 per cent for loans from official creditors such as governments and multilateral institutions. Private lenders also offered an average repayment period of 12 years, compared with 25 years for official creditors. item.title: 2027: Security tops as APC-PCC unveils 4-point manifesto
item.description: By Soni Daniel, Emma Ujah & Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA—The Presidency yesterday asked Nigerians to study the past and current manifestoes of the All Progressives Congress, APC, and judge the party by the promises it has kept since 2023 when it assumed power. Read Also: Security of lives and property to top Tinubu’s agenda in 2nd term – APC The Presidential Campaign Council, APC-PCC, also said President Bola Tinubu will pay priority attention to protection of lives and property if he wins the presidential election on January 16, 2027. Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, who made the declaration at the unveiling of the APC manifesto, titled ‘’From Reforms to Prosperity,’’ described the manifesto as a binding pact with the electorate. “A manifesto, in its strictest sense, is simply a contract between the people and their leaders. It is an inviolable contract, and we take the strict interpretation of what a manifesto represents as gospel under this administration,” he said. He admitted that the reforms had put real pressure on households, adding that the people living through it deserve to be heard. “Nobody should have to pretend that life is easy at the moment,” he said. The former House of Representatives’ Speaker, nonetheless, defended President Tinubu’s decision to act, saying the President confronted the subsidy burden and a distorted foreign exchange system when he took responsibility for the country in 2023. He said: “Leaving those problems untouched would have continued to weaken our ability to invest in the future. The difference between a politician and a leader is that while a politician thinks about the next election, a leader thinks about the next generation. And that is exactly what President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has demonstrated. Four pillars The manifesto rests on four pillars, including a secure and resilient nation; a better quality and more affordable life for every Nigerian; energy, infrastructure and economic growth; and effective and accountable governance. They are tied to the eight priority areas of the Renewed Hope Agenda, which the document said would be carried out on four foundations – macroeconomic stability; the rule of law; institutional capability; and national cohesion. By 2031, the document commits to power generation scaled towards 10,000 megawatts, annual economic growth of six per cent, and youth unemployment and out-of-school children, both halved. It also promises 20,000 additional teachers and health insurance expanded from more than 23 million enrollees to 40 per cent of Nigerians. Primary health centres will function in at least 90 per cent of facilities, up from the current 53 per cent. It further promises to work towards 200,000 homes under the Tinubu Mass Social Housing Scheme, Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria, FMBN, mortgages and licensed private developers, tracked on a public dashboard. item.title: I was soaked for hours before help came — 74-year-old blind man whose home was wrecked by wind storms
item.description: …Good-spirited man begins rebuilding the house By Chinedu Adonu ENUGU – For 74-year-old Mr. Stephen Ogbo, the rainstorm that ripped through his residence at Ugbo Ezeji, D-Line, Abakpa Nike, Enugu metropolis, was a terrifying, unforgettable experience. The ugly incident left him soaked in water for hours, trapped in a shattered building and unable to find his way to safety because of his blindness. As the storm raged, Ogbo could neither see the destruction around him nor find his way out. He remained helpless until an unidentified female tenant eventually came to his rescue. Recounting his ordeal, Ogbo said the woman approached him after he had spent several hours soaked in water, unable to escape from the disaster. “The female tenant came to me after several hours but couldn’t find any way to escape as a blind man. She said: “Daddy, we have been trapped by the windstorm,” he recalled. According to him, the woman held him, led him out of the destroyed building, and searched for shelter where he could find safety. Although he could not identify his rescuer, he remembered that the voice belonged to a woman. “I do not know the name of the woman who came to my rescue, but the voice was a woman’s voice,” he said. A native of Nomeh Unateze in Nkanu East Local Government Area of Enugu State, Ogbo said he had lived in the compound for about eight years before the incident. The rainstorm damaged the residential building housing 23 families, ripping off its roof and destroying property belonging to tenants. The incident left the occupants struggling to find shelter and salvage their belongings. For the affected families, what began as an ordinary evening quickly turned into a nightmare, with the destruction leaving them with the difficult task of restoring their homes and livelihoods. A cry for help However, days after the incident, help has begun to come following an appeal by the victims for help. Chief Kingsley Chizoba Nweke, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) senatorial candidate for Enugu East Senatorial District, where the blind man hails from, has commenced the reconstruction of the damaged home after watching a video in which the victims appealed for assistance. Nweke visited the affected residents at Ugbo Ezeji and said their plight moved him to intervene, and announced that building materials had been purchased and contractors mobilised to commence the reconstruction. “It’s a pity, actually. If you look at the roof, it is damaged, and the place is messed up. I saw them interviewed two days ago and they cried out that they needed help. “That touched me so much, so I said it was important that I come to their rescue. We have bought the materials, mobilized the contractors, and the work has already commenced,” he said. item.title: Asaba massacre and Gen Taiwo’s apology
item.description: The apology by retired Major-General Ahmed Ibrahim Taiwo, son of late Colonel Ibrahim Taiwo, to the people of Asaba over the 1967 massacre by federal troops is a remarkable gesture. At the 59th anniversary on October 7, 2026, Ahmed Taiwo expressed profound regret and apologised on behalf of his father and family for any act of omission or commission that contributed to the tragedy. Major Ibrahim Taiwo was the second-in-command of the Nigerian Army’s 2nd Infantry Division under the overall command of Col. Murtala Mohammed, which pushed Biafran troops out of Asaba. Historical accounts have it that on 7th October 1967, over a thousand unarmed Asaba men and boys, were assembled to chant “One Nigeria” as a declaration of their loyalty to the Federal Military Government. Major Taiwo, with Col. Mohammed’s approval, allegedly gave orders for them to be massacred. Curiously, nine years later on 13th February 1976, Mohammed, then the Military Head of State and Taiwo, his trusted aide and Military Governor of Kwara State, were assassinated in a coup plot led by Col. Buka S. Dimka, their former comrades during the Biafra War. Mohammed and Taiwo reportedly took this dastardly decision in revenge for the role played by an indigene of that area, Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu, the leader of the first military coup in Nigeria, in the murder of the Premier of Northern Nigeria, Sir Ahmadu Bello and other Northern leaders. Military officers from the area had also executed Biafra’s overrunning of the Mid-West and parts of the Western Regions before the tide turned against them. Since the War ended, Asaba people’s pains from this incident have been expressed through various means. One of these was Blood on the Nigeria, a bestseller authored by the late ace journalist, Chief Emma Okocha. The apology, coming from a retired senior military officer, is particularly significant. Rather than defend his father against historical accusations, Gen Taiwo chose acknowledgement, contrition and reconciliation. This is commendable. “I used to come online and start telling people that it happened. I would tell them, ‘My father is the one mentioned. I have all to gain by denying it, but you cannot deny what happened. It is what it is. I have come, in private capacity as Taiwo to render our deepest regrets and apologize on behalf of our father and family for any act of omission or commission on his part that led to this heinous massacre,” Taiwo said. Military necessity cannot justify such atrocities. Col. Taiwo’s son, who served meritoriously in the Nigerian Army, has now demonstrated that military loyalty and filial affection need not obstruct historical truth. Asaba’s paramount ruler, the Asagba, Professor Epiphany Azinge, accepted the apology and publicly forgave the Taiwo family. We urge the community to receive this gesture in good faith. item.title: Reductionism and the national question: From grievance to federal reform (II), by Usman Sarki
item.description: “Federalism involves the linking of individuals, groups and polities in lasting but limited union in such a way as to provide for the energetic pursuit of common goals while maintaining the respective integrities of all parties.” — Daniel J. Elazar If restructuring is to serve any useful national purpose, the first task must be to distinguish structural defects from failures of governance. Nigeria is excessively centralised in several respects. The Federal Government carries responsibilities that might more effectively be exercised at lower levels. The fiscal relationship among the tiers requires reconsideration. Security arrangements must reflect the reality that many threats are local. States require greater economic flexibility, while local government autonomy and accountability remain unresolved. The concentration of political competition around control of Abuja also raises the stakes of national elections to unhealthy levels. These are genuine restructuring questions. But restructuring will not automatically eliminate corruption or usher in good governance. It will not by itself produce competent governors, efficient local governments, disciplined civil services, effective policing or accountable legislatures. A badly governed region will remain badly governed merely on a larger geographical scale. This is important because constitutional engineering can become an excuse for avoiding the more uncomfortable question of the integrity of leadership. The so-called national question is therefore about considerably more than tinkering with the map of the country. Nigeria operated a regional system in the First Republic, and that arrangement produced notable achievements. The regions enjoyed substantial autonomy and developed distinctive economic, educational and administrative institutions. But the same period also experienced intense political rivalry, disputed elections and censuses, regional crises and, ultimately, the collapse of the constitutional order. The lesson is not that regionalism failed, nor that it should never be reconsidered. It is that no constitutional arrangement can substitute for political accommodation, institutional integrity and a sound democratic culture. Likewise, later state-creation exercises addressed some minority fears and brought government closer to previously neglected areas. But the multiplication of states also created new minorities, new boundary disputes, fresh grievances, demands for additional states, wastefulness and a high cost of governance. Political structures solve some problems while creating others. That reality should encourage equilibrium and rationality in the restructuring debate. item.title: Spurring Ebonyi’s shy momentum, by Ochereome Nnanna
item.description: Ebonyi State is on my mind today for a reason. On 1st October 2026, it celebrated its 30th anniversary under the helmsmanship of Governor Francis Ogbonna Nwifuru. The late Head of State, General Sani Abacha, created six new states from each of the newly designated geopolitical zones: Ebonyi, Ekiti, Bayelsa, Nasarawa, Gombe and Zamfara. Interestingly, Nwifuru, who now sits pretty at the helm of its affairs, was only 18! Obviously, when this state was created, Nwifuru and young Ebonyians like him were tailor-made to inherit its future. The state, which was carved out of Abia and Enugu States, is the smallest by population and landmass, as well as well behind the developmental level of its four senior sisters: Abia, Imo, Enugu and Anambra. However, Ebonyi has been unusually blessed with a string of good-performing governors since 1999. On this score, only Enugu State compares. In 1999, Dr Sam Egwu, a crop scientist and celebrated academic, emerged as the first elected governor. Egwu plunged headlong into education and agriculture, establishing the Ebonyi State University. After his eight years, he handed over to a veteran administrator, Chief Martin Elechi. Elechi’s main legacies were the construction of roads and 39 “Bridges of Unity” across the state. Elechi also handed over to his former Deputy Governor, Dave Umahi, a megalomaniac who also went on to display his craft as a construction engineer, building massive institutions, including city roads, flyovers, markets, an airport (though poorly done), and the Federal University Teaching Hospital, which he painted in riotous colours and named after himself. Umahi’s airport was later abandoned, and Nwifuru had to reconstruct the runway. The revolving chair eventually settled on Rt. Hon. Francis Ogbonna Nwifuru, who served as the two-term Speaker of the Ebonyi State House of Assembly. No other Ebonyi Speaker was able to serve beyond one term. Nwifuru’s story is a classic “grass to grace” tale. He was once a mason (bricklayer). But he attended the Ebonyi State University and specialised in the building sciences. He is determined to prove his trade through concrete examples (forgive the pun). While his predecessors concentrated on the big roads and bridges, Nwifuru has chosen to fix his efforts on the interconnecting rural roads which take the people home right to their communities. He launched his 115 “two-kilometres-each” roads, complete with bridges and culverts. Many of them have been completed, while the rest are assignments for his envisaged second term in office. The logic behind this strategy is impeccable. Ebonyi State, small as it is by landmass, is one of the frontline agrarian states in the country, with its native population renowned for their deep agricultural traditions. These two-kilometre roads, when completed, will link between 230 and 300 rural communities and enable them to evacuate their agricultural products to commercial centres. item.title: US midterms: True democracy at work
item.description: By SUNNY IKHIOYA Should democracy be the rightful route to leadership? That has been the question since the time of the early philosophers. Socrates (470–399 BC), the father of Greek philosophy, argued: “Democracy must fall because it will try to tailor to everyone. The poor will want the wealth of the rich, and democracy will give it to them. Young people will want to be respected as elderly, and democracy will give it to them. Women will want to be like men, and democracy will give it to them. Foreigners will want the rights of the natives, and democracy will give it to them. Thieves and fraudsters will want important government functions, and democracy will give it to them. And at that time, when thieves and fraudsters finally democratically take authority because criminals and evildoers want power, there will be worse dictatorship than in the time of any monarchy or oligarchy.” As recently as August 12, 2026, former President Olusegun Obasanjo asked whether there was such a thing as African democracy. He concluded: “Let us not deceive ourselves, there is nothing like African democracy. We were given Western liberal democracy by our colonial masters. Western liberal democracy that we inherited pulls from monarchy, hence we can have a government and a loyal opposition, loyal to the monarchy. But when you talk about loyal opposition in an African setting — and I have gone into many African languages — opposition means enemy. That is the word.” With the recent US midterm elections, people all over the world are beginning to believe again that democracy is practicable, if done in the right manner. The United States has shown again that it remains the leading democratic nation in the world — no one comes close — despite its wobbling and fumbling. Man, by nature, is flawed, but strong structures and institutions keep him in check. Democracy says the people’s voice must decide leadership. Sometimes, out of emotion, the choices turn out badly, as we witnessed in the decision to bring in Donald Trump. But the beauty of real democracy is that the same system allows the people to correct their mistakes in subsequent electoral cycles. That is what we have just witnessed. A strong, overbearing and intimidating presidency was brought to its knees by what was assumed to be a passive opposition party. But the people had their say, and that will remain the will of the American people until the next general election. Many people, especially those of us from this part of the world, have come to see democracy as a scam — a game of the powerful elite, the military, business oligarchs and their cronies imposing their will on the people. We see elections as a do-or-die affair, with extreme religious and ethnic sentiments on full display. True democracy is real, and the US has just shown it. item.title: At Beyond the Ballot Summit, ALTON pledges a resilient telecom network, by Okoh Aihe
item.description: Concluding her keynote on Beyond the Ballot Summit in Abuja, Prof Abigail Ogwezzy-Ndisika wrote: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Foreign Information Manipulation pose serious challenges to our republic but they are not our destiny because technology is created by humans and human institutions retain the moral authority, legal mandate and practical capacity to defend the truth. Concerning the 2027 Election, this hints at shared human responsibility to manage technology especially in this age of AI to enable it deliver instead of permitting its adulteration that can lead to unsavory results. When Ogwezzy-Ndisika presented her very pedantic paper, Beyond the Ballot: Architectural Resilience, Generative AI and Securing Electoral Integrity for Nigeria 2027 Polls, both Gbenga Adebayo, ALTON Chairman, and Seun Okinbaloye of Channels Television, were not present in the opening day. On the second day however, they had to tackle each other on how human handling of technology can guaranty fidelity of the electoral process. The nation has a point of reference that is not inspiring. Just when everybody thought the 2023 Presidential Election was on a smooth sail, and boom, came a technical glitch that rendered it difficult for information from the polling stations to be uploaded for onward transmission. A beautiful election had been blighted within seconds, raising tension across the nation. With the stubborn intrusion of Artificial Intelligence, the organizers of the Summit, IPC, CEMESO and DAI, with support from the EU Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria (EU-SDGN), had history in mind but they were also very conscious of how to manage the entire gamut of technology, including AI, to deliver trusted election results. Hold democracy together and be able to create more human development that can impact technological growth for humanity instead of phobia for the unknown. The second day came with significant highlights. It was the Panel Session on Telecoms Accountability and Responsible Influencing: What Should Telecom operators and Influencers Do Differently in 2027? The Session featuring Adebayo of ALTON, Dan Bello and Rukayya Muhammed, two Social Media influencers, was moderated by Okinbaloye. Almost pressed beyond limits by Okinbaloye on whether the government could shut down the telecom network for whatever reason, Adebayo contributed that there were regulatory issues and cognate developments that could be responsible for such a situation but his conclusion being that the government cannot shut down the network. This I totally agreed with because no matter what you may want to accuse the Bola Tinubu government of, one thing I can say is that it is not a rogue government that may want to act irresponsibly without recourse to the law of the land. item.title: FG coming with major agric reforms to boost food production, cut inflation — ADENLE
item.description: The Federal Government (FG) has proposed sweeping reforms in the agricultural sector, including digitalisation, mechanisation and improved coordination among government agencies in the sector, to boost food production, reduce food inflation and strengthen food security. Senior Special Adviser on Agricultural Innovation to the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, Professor Ademola Adenle, disclosed this in an interview where he outlined plans to resolve long-standing challenges in the sector. Adenle said digitalisation will help government identify genuine farmers, monitor production, ensure transparent distribution of inputs and expand farmers’ access to markets. He said the National Agricultural Growth initiative had introduced a system where agro-dealers distribute inputs to verified farmers while monitoring their output. According to him, the intervention has increased production by 30%, with wheat output rising from 420,000 tonnes to 480,000 tonnes annually. He, however, admitted that higher production alone would not bring down food prices unless institutional weaknesses and structural inefficiencies were addressed. “Previous programmes focused mainly on production and input distribution without addressing institutional capacity, food security and agro-industrialisation,” he said. Adenle called for an overhaul of the ministry’s administrative and legal structures, noting that bureaucratic bottlenecks had limited the impact of interventions. He identified poor coordination among federal, state and local governments as a major challenge, and advocated harmonised agricultural policies across the three tiers. He also proposed performance-based financing, annual key performance indicators, stronger monitoring and evaluation, data-driven decision-making, and legislation to promote accountability and transparency. On rising food prices, Adenle blamed illegal movement of produce across Nigeria’s borders and hoarding of food commodities for creating artificial scarcity. He said the Nigeria Customs Service and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission are working with security agencies to address the problem. item.title: Climate plans: CAPPA warns against fossil fuel expansion, corporate capture
item.description: … Says Nigeria’s 2060 net-zero ambition contradicts 3m barrels-per-day oil target … Demands phase-down of fossil fuels, grants, protection of community land rights By Chioma Obinna Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) on Tuesday warned that African governments risk turning their climate commitments into instruments for expanding fossil fuel production and advancing corporate interests at the expense of vulnerable communities. The organisation, alongside the Africa Make Big Polluters Pay Coalition (MBPP Africa), said Africa’s climate transition would amount to little more than rhetoric unless governments confronted the contradictions between their renewable energy commitments, continued investments in oil and gas, and growing dependence on foreign climate financing. The warning came as the organisations unveiled two reports examining Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan and the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) of five African countries at a media presentation in Lagos. The reports, titled Four Years On: Examining Nigeria’s Just Transition Plan and Nationally Determined Contributions in Africa: A Five-Country Policy Analysis, assessed the climate commitments of Nigeria, Cameroon, South Africa, Togo and Uganda. They identified fossil fuel expansion, uncertain climate financing, carbon markets and the growing influence of private corporations in climate policy development as major threats to achieving a genuinely just transition across the continent. Speaking, the Executive Director of CAPPA, Akinbode Oluwafemi, said the central question was whether African climate policies were genuinely transforming economies and protecting people or creating fresh opportunities for corporate interests to profit while communities bear the consequences. He said: “These reports emerge from a fundamental concern: Are Africa’s climate policies genuinely transforming our economies and protecting our people, or are they creating new opportunities for corporate interests to profit while communities bear the consequences?” Oluwafemi said governments could not claim to be pursuing decarbonisation while simultaneously approving projects and infrastructure that entrenched dependence on fossil fuels. He cited the contradictions in Uganda, where French multinational TotalEnergies promotes investments in renewable energy, including solar, while remaining a leading developer of the East African Crude Oil Pipeline, EACOP, and the Tilenga oil project. He also referenced Cameroon’s award of five of nine oil blocks offered to fossil fuel operators, including Murphy Oil and Octavia Energy, despite its stated decarbonisation commitments. In Nigeria, the report identified a major contradiction between the country’s ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2060 and its official target of producing three million barrels of crude oil daily by 2030. item.title: Agbazuere backs Otti’s second-term bid after U-turn
item.description: Dismisses alleged anti-Ngwa remark, cautions critics By Steve Oko UMUAHIA—Former Chief of Staff to ex-Governor Okezie Ikpeazu, Prof. ACB Agbazuere, who was a vocal critic of Governor Alex Otti during the 2019 governorship election, has declared support for the governor’s re-election bid, saying he deserves a second term. Agbazuere, now a member of Otti’s Campaign Advisory Council, also dismissed an allegation attributed to former Commissioner, Chief Charles Ogbonnaya, that the governor allegedly described Ngwa people as brainless, describing the claim as unfounded and politically motivated. Speaking during a radio interview simulcast across several stations in Abia on Tuesday, Agbazuere cautioned politicians against making unsubstantiated allegations, warning that defamatory statements could attract legal consequences under Nigerian laws, including the Cybercrimes Act. He said the allegation would not undermine Otti’s support base, particularly among the Ngwa people. “Dr Alex Otti may love peace; Dr Alex Otti may not want trouble, but they should see that people like us are now with him. Anybody who wants to say anything should be careful and say what he knows to be true,” he warned. Explaining his support for the governor, Agbazuere said the Otti administration had demonstrated commitment to infrastructure development, urban renewal, workers’ welfare and good governance. He cited the reconstruction of Port Harcourt Road and Bank Road in Aba, the Omenuko Bridge and Arochukwu Road as evidence of the administration’s infrastructure drive. He also commended the governor for what he described as regular payment of salaries, pensions and gratuities, as well as improvements in allowances for traditional rulers. On criticisms that increased federal allocations should have translated into more development projects, Agbazuere argued that the rising cost of construction materials must be considered. He cited the increase in the price of cement from about ₦2,000 to ₦12,000 per bag as an example of the inflationary pressures facing construction projects. He challenged critics to visit the state and assess ongoing projects rather than evaluate the administration from a distance. Describing Otti as a banker and trained economist, Agbazuere said the governor understood accountability and prudent management of public resources. He urged Abians to look beyond party affiliations and support continuity, arguing that a second term would enable Otti to complete ongoing projects and consolidate his administration’s programmes. He also recalled that during the 2023 governorship election, a leading opposition candidate had reportedly acknowledged Otti as the best candidate. Vanguard reports that Agbazuere, a former Commissioner for Information, was previously among Otti’s vocal critics but has recently switched allegiance after leaving the All Progressives Congress (APC), where he briefly sought political shelter shortly after Otti assumed office in 2023. item.title: Tinubu Won 2023 Election On His Own, Buhari Didn’t Fully Support Him – APC’s Hassan
item.description: A spokesperson for the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, Alwan Hassan, has said President Bola Tinubu won the 2023 presidential election against all odds, insisting that former President Muhammadu Buhari did not fully support his candidacy. Hassan said Tinubu secured victory largely through his own political strength, arguing that Buhari did not actively stand behind the APC candidate during the build-up to the election. He made the remarks on Tuesday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today , while discussing the president’s chances of securing re-election in 2027. During the interview, Hassan was asked whether Tinubu would benefit from the organic political structure and support base associated with his predecessor, particularly as the APC prepares for another presidential contest in the next two months. In response, the APC stalwart questioned whether Buhari had given Tinubu the full backing of his political structure in 2023. “Did he enjoy that in 2023? Did we enjoy Buhari’s support in 2023? Let the truth be told, we did not,” he said. ﻿ When asked whether he was suggesting that Tinubu won the 2023 election on his own, Hassan answered in the affirmative, maintaining that the former president did not fully support his successor’s ambition. “On his own. Buhari didn’t fully come out to support Tinubu,” he said. He further argued that Buhari did not actively campaign for Tinubu during the 2023 election, despite both politicians belonging to the same political party. “Buhari didn’t do well in 2023. He didn’t actually come out to stand for us and stand for Asiwaju in 2023. Asiwaju won that election against all odds,” Hassan said. item.title: [VIDEO] Wike’s ₦10m Pledge: INEC, Police Can Trigger Investigation, Says Okoye
item.description: A former National Commissioner of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Festus Okoye, says the commission, the police and other law enforcement agencies can initiate an investigation into the ₦10 million pledge by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, to councillors ahead of the 2027 general elections. Okoye, a lawyer, said this on Tuesday while appearing as a guest on Channels Television’s Politics Today. He said the absence of action by INEC would not prevent individuals or other relevant authorities from raising concerns or investigating the matter if an electoral offence was suspected. “If INEC is not taking this up, can anyone petition on this matter to say, I think Minister Wike is doing the wrong thing? Is it possible? Oh, definitely, yes,” he said. ﻿ The ex-commissioner added that the state could also initiate action if an offence had been committed, while law enforcement agencies could investigate where they believed there were grounds to suspect a violation. Mr Okoye said INEC could equally petition the relevant authorities to investigate the matter and prosecute anyone found culpable. Wike had pledged ₦10 million to each FCT councillor who successfully delivers their ward for President Bola Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the 2027 elections. item.title: NDC Alleges Plot To Disrupt Obi’s Benue Visit, Govt Denies Claim
item.description: The Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) has accused the Benue State Government of plotting to disrupt the planned visit of its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, to the state, an allegation the government has dismissed as false. Obi is scheduled to visit Benue State on Wednesday for a town hall meeting in Makurdi and a humanitarian visit to Yelewata, where he is expected to pay tribute to victims of the June 2025 massacre and commiserate with their families. Addressing journalists in Makurdi on Tuesday, the party’s governorship candidate in the state, Terhemba Shija, called on the state government and security agencies to guarantee the safety of Obi and his supporters. Shija alleged that the government had issued threats aimed at preventing the former Anambra State governor from visiting Yelewata, recalling an earlier attempt to stop him from visiting the community. He said the party had notified the state government and security agencies of the planned visit, adding that its arrangements were already in place. “This letter addressed to His Excellency, the Executive Governor of Benue, was received on the 10th of November, which is today. “While we discuss with the security agency, all they require is that we should send them an itinerary of our visit. I’m going to soon embark on the visit of all the local governments. All I have told the DG to do is to write the itinerary, the times that we’ll be here, and then they will follow,” he said, displaying a copy of the correspondence. ﻿ Shija maintained that the party did not require permission from the state government to conduct its political activities but had notified the authorities in the interest of a peaceful visit. He described Obi’s planned trip as both humanitarian and political, saying the presidential candidate would lay a wreath at the cenotaph erected in memory of the victims of the Yelewata massacre along the Lafia Road. The NDC governorship candidate said Obi would also meet relatives of the victims but would not visit any government facility or internally displaced persons’ camp. According to him, the town hall meeting would be held at the multipurpose hall of the Mission House in Makurdi, behind the Benue Links head office in Wurukum. Shija alleged that the state government was unhappy with Obi’s visit because of its potential political implications ahead of the 2027 general elections. He also accused the government of being behind an earlier attempt to disrupt the presidential candidate’s visit to Yelewata, claiming that suspected supporters of the slogan, “No Alia, No Benue”, had mobilised to prevent him from accessing the community. He, however, urged Obi’s supporters to remain vigilant and peaceful, insisting that the party would not be deterred by the alleged threats. “The visit of Mr Peter Obi is going to be conducted in a peaceful atmosphere. item.title: Makinde Presents ₦1.115tn 2027 Budget To Oyo Assembly
item.description: Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, has presented a proposed budget of ₦1.115 trillion for the 2027 fiscal year to the State House of Assembly for consideration and approval. Tagged the “Budget of Sustained Progress”, the proposal is valued at ₦1,115,341,378,359.90. Presenting the budget on Tuesday at the Assembly complex in Agodi, Ibadan, Makinde said it was designed to consolidate the gains of his administration and lay a foundation for sustainable development beyond its tenure. He described it as the final budget proposal of his administration, saying it would sustain the state’s development momentum and ensure continuity after the transition to a new government. “As we prepare to hand over the baton to the next administration, we bring before you the 2027 Budget of Sustained Progress. It is designed to consolidate our gains, sustain public services and carry our state’s development forward through the transition period and beyond,” he said. The governor said the proposal prioritised infrastructure, community development and the strengthening of public institutions, with significant allocations for capital projects in health, education and road infrastructure. He added that his administration was committed to leaving behind clear records, properly documented processes and institutions capable of sustaining efficient service delivery. Highlighting his administration’s achievements, Makinde said Oyo State’s Internally Generated Revenue increased by 288 per cent, from ₦26.59 billion in 2019 to ₦103.25 billion in 2025. He also noted that the state ranked third nationally in the 2025 Subnational Ease of Doing Business Assessment. The governor said targeted interventions and partnerships had helped return about 65,000 out-of-school children to classrooms, alongside investments in educational infrastructure, recruitment and service delivery. He, however, said the administration’s performance should be measured beyond revenue figures and rankings. “Figures alone cannot fully assess our administration. The real measure of success is the impact we have made on the lives of our people and the institutions we have built to serve them beyond May 29, 2027,” he said. Makinde also reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to women’s inclusion in governance, pledging to sustain the 35 per cent affirmative action policy for women. On infrastructure and agriculture, he said the government had prioritised strategic road projects to connect economic corridors, improve market access and create opportunities for farmers, businesses and rural communities. He said the establishment of the Oyo State Agribusiness Development Agency had helped reposition agriculture as a viable business sector, while the Oyo State Agribusiness Transformation Centre had become a hub for agricultural investment.
